title: The Triple S and the Jalebi Betrayal
paras: Thursday, July 27, 2006.

That’s the day I, Sayali, entered this chaotic world. I came straight from the womb to the "Mother Hospital" in Beed, Maharashtra. I don’t know if my parents were happy in that exact moment, but I guess they had to be—I was the second installment in the "Triple S" franchise.
My father, Pandit Tikaram Rathod, had a vision. He wanted a brand, a legacy. So he named us all with ‘S’: Satish, Sayali, Suraj.

It sounds cute, like a team of superheroes. In reality, it was just a hierarchy of chaos. There was Satish, the eldest, who I am convinced has a split personality. In front of our parents, he is the model son; the moment they leave the room, he transforms into a completely different person. Then there is Suraj, the baby. And then there is me—the middle child, the sandwich.

To understand my life, you have to understand "The Management." First, there is Pappa. He is a simple man, strict but somehow... bland. He was the type of father who was physically present but emotionally on mute. While other dads played catch, Pappa checked our grades.

Then, there is Mummy. If Pappa was the ghost, Mummy was the Warden. She was always there. She didn't give us space; she gave us rules. If I wanted to play outside or visit a friend, I didn't just ask permission—I had to file a legal petition, cry for hours, and promise my soul. Even then, the answer was usually "No."
But Pappa had one redeeming quality. One "love language" that we all understood: The Jalebi.

We lived in a house that sat on top of a charcoal depot—literally. Our family business supplied charcoal to restaurants and hotels, so our home was always perched above a mountain of black dust. The road outside wasn't a road; it was a village trail of dirt, jagged stones, and marbles.
It was a ritual. Whenever Pappa went out for work, he would bring back snacks.
Specifically, Jalebi—Mummy’s favorite. It was the only way we knew he loved her. One morning, i think it was 2011, the ritual went wrong.

Pappa arrived on his bike, the smell of sweet fried sugar drifting from the bags. I was very small back then—tiny enough that Pappa lifted me up and set me on the trunk of his parked bike while he sorted things out. I sat there like a queen on her throne, waiting for my share of the sweets.
But then, Pappa walked away. Maybe he was distracted by work, or maybe he just forgot I was there (middle child problems).
I didn’t know how to get down. I wobbled. I tipped. And then—gravity won.
I fell headfirst off the bike, straight onto that jagged, stone-filled road. Crack. A single marble, buried in the dirt, met my forehead with perfect aim.

Blood started gushing. I started screaming. Pappa came running back, scooping me up in his arms like a hero in a slow-motion movie scene. He was terrified. He was running toward the house, ready to get me help.
But through the blood and the tears, I grabbed his shirt. I didn't care about the hole in my head. I didn't care about the pain. I looked him in the eye and whispered the only thing that mattered:
"Don't take me to Mummy. She will scold me."
That is the terror Mrs. Rathod inspired. I had a marble stuck in my skull, but I was more afraid of her anger than I was of bleeding out.

To this day, I have a bald spot on my head where the hair refuses to grow—a permanent souvenir. It’s a reminder of the day I fell, and the day I realized that in the Rathod household, fear of Mummy was stronger than the fear of death.

title: The White Flood & The Great Betrayal
paras: If there is one rule in an Indian household, it is this: Do not mess with the milk. Milk is sacred. It is for tea, for growing bones, and apparently, for creating absolute disasters.

It was a typical afternoon. Bhaiya (Satish) and I had just dragged ourselves home from school. We were exhausted, our backpacks felt like they weighed a ton, and our stomachs were making noises that sounded like dying whales. We were starving. We walked into the kitchen, and there it was—the Holy Grail. Mummy had left a massive container of milk on the gas stove to boil.

Now, this wasn't a cup of milk. This was a vessel. It was filled to the brim, steaming hot, and radiating heat like a mini-sun. A rational person would look at that bubbling lava and think, "I should wait for an adult."
But we were not rational. We were hungry.
"I got this," Bhaiya said.
Famous last words. Bhaiya, being Bhaiya, decided he didn't need a ladle or a cup. He decided to lift the entire heavy, scorching vessel himself.
It happened in slow motion. His hands slipped. The vessel tilted.
SPLASH.
A tsunami of boiling white liquid crashed onto the kitchen counter and cascaded onto the floor. The kitchen wasn't a kitchen anymore; it was a swimming pool of Amul’s finest.
Panic set in immediately. The pain of the heat was nothing compared to the chilling realization of what was coming next: Mummy.
"She’s going to kill us," I whispered. "She is actually going to kill us."
But we had a potential savior. Our Maushi (the maid).
She was in the other room, and she had heard the crash. We ran to her like refugees seeking asylum. We begged. We pleaded. We offered the ultimate bribe:
"Maushi, please! If you clean this up before Mummy comes home, we promise we won’t bother you for a whole month. We’ll be angels. Just please, make the milk disappear!"
Maushi looked at the mess. She looked at our terrified faces. She nodded. We had a deal. A sacred pact.
She wiped up the floor. The kitchen looked spotless. We breathed a sigh of relief. We had survived. The crime scene was clean.

Then, Mummy came home from the shop. She looked tired. She sat down, and Maushi walked over to her. They started talking in low voices—the kind of "women’s talk" that usually involves gossip or grocery prices. Bhaiya and I sat in the corner, exchanging confident looks. We are safe, we thought. The deal is holding.
Suddenly, Maushi pointed a finger at us.
"And you won't believe what these two did today..." she said.

My heart stopped. She flipped. She didn't just tell the truth; she gave a detailed report of the crime! The betrayal cut deeper than any knife. We looked at her with wide eyes—What about the deal? What about the month of peace?!
Mummy’s eyes shifted from Maushi to us. The tiredness vanished from her face, replaced by the familiar "Rathod Wrath."
That day, we didn't get dinner. We got the "chappal treatment."
As I sat there crying, rubbing my arm, I learned a valuable lesson: Never trust a Maushi who has a better relationship with your mother than you do.

title: The Trilogy & The Extra Wheel
paras: Before we had the charcoal depot house, we lived in an apartment in Aurangabad. It was the "Struggle Era"—the time when my parents were just starting their careers in coal. But we weren't struggling alone.
We shared our world with two other families who were building their lives right alongside us: The Dhole Family and The Kumbhakarna Family.
(Yes, "Kumbhakarna" is their real surname. No, they didn't sleep for six months at a time like the mythological giant, though that would have been cool).
While my Pappa was dealing with black coal, the other fathers were carving out their own paths.
Govind Uncle (Dhole family) owned a medical store—which was honestly very convenient considering how often we kids scraped our knees.

Shivaji Uncle (Kumbhakarna family) had the most inspiring climb. He started his career as a painter, adding color to walls, but through sheer hard work, he eventually rose to become a Manager at Electric City.
Looking back, our three families were weirdly synchronized. It was like the Universe was copy-pasting our lives.
Phase 1: The Boys (The "S" Squad) In 2004, the universe decided to drop three boys into the apartment block.
My brother, Satish.
Saurav Dhole.
Shivam Kumbhakarna.

It wasn't a planned "Triple S" franchise like my dad wanted; it was just a spooky coincidence. These three grew up together, breathing the same air, sharing the same toys, and probably breaking the same windows. They were the original trio.

Phase 2: The Girl Gang Then came my turn. I arrived in 2006. But this time, the other aunties weren't pregnant... yet. The "Girl Gang" was under construction. I vividly remember watching the aunties’ bellies grow, waiting for my future best friends to arrive.
In 2007, Gauri Dhole (daughter of Govind uncle and Anita Aunty) joined the chat. In 2008, Pragati Kumbhakarna (daughter of Shivaji uncle and Sharadha Aunty) completed the set.

It was perfect symmetry. The fathers were friends. The mothers were friends. The boys had their gang. The girls had our gang. The Dhole family was full (Saurav + Gauri). The Kumbhakarna family was full (Shivam + Pragati).
And then... there was the Rathod family.
Phase 3: The "Extra" My parents apparently didn't get the memo that we were supposed to stop at two. Enter Suraj.

Because the other families had "closed their bookings," poor Suraj had no counterpart. There was no "Baby Dhole" or "Baby Kumbhakarna" for him to play with. He was the odd number. The spare part. The "Extra."
And because he had no friends of his own, he decided his full-time job was to annoy me.

Suraj is four years younger than me. In kid years, that is a lifetime. But whenever I planned a sophisticated outing with Gauri and Pragati—probably to discuss very serious toddler business—Suraj would be standing at the door, crying his eyes out. "I want to go too! Take me!"
I would look at Mummy, begging her with my eyes to save me. Please, Mummy. He’s small. He’s annoying. He’s Extra.
But Mummy, the Supreme Court Judge of the household, would bang her gavel and deliver the sentence I dreaded most:
"If you want to go, you have to take him along. Otherwise, you stay home."
End of discussion.

So, there we would be: three cool girls trying to have a girl gang moment, and one crying, snotty-nosed little brother trailing behind us, ruining the vibe. He was the tax I had to pay for my freedom.

title: The Geopolitics of a Neon Fairy T-Shirt
paras: There is a fundamental flaw in the way older siblings view younger siblings. They expect you to instantly possess the exact same amount of wisdom they have, completely ignoring the fact that they have a multi-year head start.

When I was about ten years old, Bhaiya was twelve. That two-year gap meant he felt he was an enlightened philosopher, while I was just trying to survive the fifth grade. He expected me to be as mature as he was, forgetting that whatever he had learned in the last twenty-four months, I wouldn't learn for another two years.

One day, Bhaiya and I were sitting on the terrace. I was wearing my absolute favorite T- shirt: a pristine, full-white tee featuring a neon green fairy. I was leaning comfortably against the sharp corner of a concrete pillar, just chilling.

Somehow, our casual sibling chatter shifted to international relations. Politics. Countries. Now, keeping in mind that I was a ten-year-old kid who only knew what she overheard adults saying, I casually mentioned that Pakistan and China were "bad." I had no political nuance; I was just parroting the environment around me. It’s what kids do before they grow up and realize the world isn't black and white.
Well, Bhaiya, in his infinite twelve-year-old wisdom, strongly disagreed with my geopolitical stance.
I don't know what snapped in his brain, but instead of offering a calm, educational counter-argument, he opted for physical violence. He literally kicked me in the face.
The force threw me backward, and the back of my head slammed directly into the sharp edge of the pillar I was resting against.

Pain exploded in my skull. I started crying instantly. Within seconds, my pristine white, neon-fairy T-shirt was soaking up blood, turning a terrifying shade of red. That is the exact moment Bhaiya realized he had made a huge mistake. His "tough guy" philosophical persona vanished, replaced by sheer, unadulterated panic.

He knew exactly what was about to happen if Mummy saw my bloody head. The wrath of Mrs. Rathod would descend upon him like a hurricane. Suddenly, my tormentor became my best friend. He pulled me into a tight, desperate hug as I sobbed.
"Don't tell Mummy," he pleaded, rushing to strip off my favorite T-shirt. He frantically washed the blood out of the fabric before anyone could see the evidence.

Even though my head was throbbing, I was actually mature enough to do the math: if I told Mummy, Bhaiya would get beaten terribly, and Mummy would be in a terrified frenzy. So, I made the sacrifice. I agreed to the pact of silence.
But the cover-up required a high level of endurance. At ten years old, I didn't comb my own hair yet. Mummy did it for me daily.

For days, the wound on the back of my head stayed raw and hidden beneath my hair. Every single morning, Mummy would take the comb and drag it right across my scalp. The pain was agonizing. I would bite my lip, clench my fists, and bear it in total silence just to save my brother from her wrath. I was a silent martyr for sibling solidarity.
And the best part? Today, when I remind Bhaiya about how I bravely saved him from certain doom, he doesn't thank me.
He just smirks and says, "You’re welcome. Hitting your head on that pillar is what made you smarter. You were clueless before that."

title: Black Magic, Boys, and the Lonavala Betrayal
paras: My educational journey started off like a chaotic tour of the city’s preschools.

First, I went to a pre-primary school owned by the wife of our milkman. We called him "Savai Kaka," so naturally, I was getting my ABCs and my daily dairy from the same family empire. Then, for Nursery and Senior KG, I moved to Kids Capital English School, the most famous spot in our locality for tiny humans.

For first and second grade, I upgraded to Saint Meera School. It was huge, about two kilometers from home, and felt like a whole new world. But my stay there was short-lived. Govind Uncle (Gauri’s dad) recommended Jigisha International School because Gauri and her brother Saurav were already there.
I was thrilled. I thought Gauri and I would finally rule the classroom together. But knowing my luck, we were put in completely different divisions from third all the way to eighth grade.
Despite the separation, I thrived. I was the textbook definition of a "good kid."

From third to tenth grade, I consistently scored over 90%. I didn't just attend school; I owned it. The teachers loved me, and I still miss many of them today. At the top of that list is my principal, Mrs. Manisha Nath.

In a weird twist of fate, she had been the principal at Saint Meera, and then she became the principal at Jigisha. It was like she transferred schools just to keep an eye on me. She still remembers me today, right down to what I looked like in the first grade.
Finally, in ninth and tenth grade, the universe aligned: Gauri and I were in the same class. We formed a solid squad of four: Me, Gauri, Anandi, and... Arpita.

Now, I need to explain the dynamic. I was a very shy, innocent teenager. I didn't like using bad words, and I had absolutely zero interest in boys. I just wanted to hang out with my friends. Arpita, on the other hand, was the Devil.

She was the wedge in my friendship with Gauri. I was highly possessive of my best friend, and Arpita was always swooping in, dragging Gauri away, and talking about all the things I hated. Whenever I got mad at Gauri for entertaining this, she would brush me off: "What's your problem? We are all friends, blah blah blah." I honestly believe Arpita had done some sort of black magic on her. It was the only logical explanation.This simmering tension all came to a head at the very end of tenth grade during our final school trip to Lonavala.

Getting permission for this trip was a mission. Gauri and I had to beg, plead, and campaign for two straight days before our parents finally broke down and said yes. I was ecstatic. I had this grand, cinematic vision of what the trip would be: making lifelong memories, staying up late, dancing, and bonding.

We visited Tiger Point, Imagica, the Wax Museum, and even a Ghost House. The days were actually incredibly fun. But the nights? That’s where the betrayal happened. On our first night in the hotel, the four of us were sharing a room. I was ready for the ultimate sleepover. I had plans. We were going to play Uno. We were going to laugh until our stomachs hurt.
Instead, the Devil struck. Arpita, obsessed as always, convinced Gauri to spend the evening video-calling boys.

I sat there, watching them giggle at a phone screen, absolutely fuming. We are in Lonavala to make memories with each other, and you want to sit here and watch other people enjoy themselves? What the hell? I was so disgusted and heartbroken that I just went to sleep. They didn't even try to wake me up. I had expected better from Gauri.
I stayed mad for the rest of the trip. When it was time to get back on the bus to go home, I refused to share a seat with Gauri. I sat with Anandi instead.

As the bus rolled through the dark, Anandi and I put on our earphones and listened to lo-fi songs all the way back. Staring out the dark window, watching the world pass by while the music played, felt like absolute heaven. It was exactly the kind of peace I needed after the Uno Betrayal. To this day, I still listen to that exact playlist. It’s called "Sukoon Vibes."
And by the way, if I bring this up to Gauri today, she will instantly invent fifty different excuses to justify her behavior. But I don't care.
So, Gauri, if you are reading this book right now: Mind it. I am still not over it.

title: Welcome to Kota — Hostels, Heartbreak, and the 17th Birthday
paras: After the Lonavala trip, my board exams went well, and I found myself in that weird limbo phase of waiting for results and figuring out the rest of my life.

Bhaiya had already gone to Kota, Rajasthan, for his studies. At first, I wasn't ready to leave home. Pappa and I looked for coaching centers locally in Aurangabad. I even passed the entrance exam for Swami Vivekanand College in Latur, earning free admission. But because their JEE staff was new, we ultimately made the classic Indian middle-class decision: we chose the "Mecca" of competitive exams. I was going to Kota.

I joined RELIABLE classes and moved into a hostel called Vasanti Residency, the exact same place Bhaiya used to live. And because the universe has a highly twisted sense of humor, guess who was already living in my hostel? Arpita. The Devil from Lonavala.

She was sharing a room with Sanskruti, a girl from our hometown. Fortunately, Pappa had insisted I get a single room, claiming I wouldn't study with a roommate. As the JEE journey began, I started talking to Arpita and Sanskruti. My bond with Sanskruti grew much stronger; Arpita and I had too much baggage, but with Sanskruti, I had a clean slate. We even became gym buddies, hitting the hostel basement gym together for a solid month. As time passed, Sanskruti started noticing what I already knew: Arpita was a terrible friend. She would vent to me about Arpita’s behaviour, and I would just nod, silently thinking, I told you so.
But knowing my luck, this peace didn't last. Right before my 17th birthday, Arpita and I got into a massive fight.

Now, logically, you would think Sanskruti would take my side, considering her recent realizations. But no. Because she and Arpita attended "Motion" coaching classes together, convenience won over loyalty. They formed an alliance and both decided to completely ice me out.
So, I spent my 17th birthday entirely alone.

I lived on the 9th floor of the hostel, and my only real comfort that day was standing on my balcony, staring out at the beautiful view of the city. In the morning, I quietly went to a nearby temple, attended my classes, and distributed chocolates to the hostel staff. It was a bleak, lonely day. But then, my saving grace stepped in: Gauri. Even from miles away in our hometown, she baked a cake just for me and celebrated my birthday over the phone. While the Devil and her sidekick ignored me in Kota, my true best friend made sure I felt special. And just like that, the year dragged on.

I went into Kota thinking JEE would be as easy as my 10th-grade boards. The syllabus quickly humbled me. I started studying at least ten hours a day, but my monthly test scores were abysmal. I was an emotional wreck. After every test, I would cry, stop eating, and shut out the world for a week.

But amidst the academic trauma, there were good people. There were the friends who kept me sane: Harshita, Kanak (whom I still talk to), Vani, Diya, and Ishika. We huddled together, solving each other's doubts and trying to survive.

And then there were the teachers—the generals of our Kota war. In 11th grade, I was lucky to have GDS Sir (Gautam Drolia), a fabulous Physics teacher, and DTS Mam (Deepti Thalia) for Physical Chemistry. By 12th grade, the roster changed. We had SKT Sir (Sandeep Kumar Tripathi) for Maths, NGE Sir (Nikhil Goenka) for Chemistry, DRM Mam for Organic Chemistry, and the legendary AKJ Sir (Ankush Jain)—the strictest, most terrifying Physics teacher of them all.

There were brief moments of light, like my 18th birthday. It was a stark contrast to my 17th. My parents came to visit. Even though the tension of my studies hung in the air, we celebrated in the hostel canteen, walked along the Kota Riverfront, and went to see the movie Jawan. For a day, we were just a normal, happy family.
But October arrived, and the Kota chapter was closing. It was time to go home and face the music.

title: The 1% Fall and the Kaju Katli Redemption
paras: I left Kota in October and came home to take my exams. The downward spiral began almost immediately.

I was completely unconfident for my first JEE Mains attempt in January, and my results proved my fears right. Pappa was unhappy, but he consoled me, reminding me I had a second attempt. Then came the board exams. I had spent my time writing endless practical books and drawing diagrams, but I knew almost nothing. The paperwork and form-filling for all these exams alone were enough to drive a person insane.
When the second JEE Mains rolled around, I failed again.

Pappa’s patience evaporated. I started tiptoeing around the house, terrified of him, hiding in my room to avoid his scolding. My cousins Aradhya and Arti were visiting for the holidays, which offered a tiny bit of distraction, but the looming dread was always there. Then, the final blow landed: Board Exam results.

All over the world, parents were proudly updating their WhatsApp statuses with their children's percentages. I stared at my screen in horror. The criteria for engineering colleges was 75%. I had missed it by exactly 1%.
My phone rang. It was Pappa. "What is the result?" he asked. The moment the numbers left my mouth, he hung up. The silence was deafening.

That evening, he called me into the living room, and my world turned upside down. I had never imagined that level of anger from my father. He yelled, and the disappointment in his voice crushed whatever was left of my spirit. I knew it was my fault, so I just stood there, completely still, absorbing every word. Mummy tried to defend her little girl, but my brain had shut down.

That night, Mummy refused to let me sleep alone in my room and made me sleep next to her. But I couldn't close my eyes. The thoughts in my head were a dark, unending loop. I felt like an absolute failure. I felt I didn't deserve to be alive.

At midnight, I slipped out of bed and went to the kitchen. I grabbed a knife. In a moment of sheer desperation, I dragged it across my hand. It bled profusely. Terrified and half- conscious, I wrapped my hand in a blanket, crawled back into bed next to Mummy, and prayed it would all just end.
But I woke up the next morning. I was still here.

A day later, Suraj saw the mark on my hand. My little brother—the one who used to cry to tag along with my friends, the "Extra" wheel—suddenly became my fierce protector. He was furious with me, but his hands were gentle as he cleaned the wound and applied medicine. "Don't you ever do this again," he warned me, threatening to tell our parents if I even thought about it.
I was entirely hopeless. Every exam I had filled out a form for felt like a devastating failure. Pappa and I weren't speaking.
And then, a sliver of light broke through the absolute darkness.
I had taken an entrance exam and given an interview for Scaler School of Technology. The results came out. I was selected.
That evening, the door to my room opened. It was Pappa. He wasn't yelling. He was holding a box of Kaju Katli—my absolute favorite sweet.

His eyes were welling up with tears. He walked over, hugged me tighter than he ever had, and started crying. For the first time in my life, I saw pure, unshielded love for me in my father’s eyes. For the first time, he kissed me on the cheek.
I was on top of the world. The pain, the failure, the darkness of the kitchen—it all washed away in that one embrace. My father was finally happy.
When they asked if I wanted to go to the college, I instantly said yes. It was my escape. It was my chance to leave the heavy, suffocating mindset of my hometown behind and start breathing again.
With a healed hand and a box of Kaju Katli in my heart, I packed my bags for a new life. On August 4th, I arrived in Bangalore.
